mappings.note: Retrieves how the clothes in the London store made him visible. Extraction; the ethics of the discovery are not in question here.
Why he was in the streets -- the boys and the burnt house. Extraction.
Mrs Hall's reading of him as eccentric is characterisation seen through another character. Not C-E2.2-LO-13: no lawlessness yet.
The empty study with money vanishing from the drawer is the genre's signature effect -- the unexplained made physical. Not LO-1: the episode's oddity is the point.
The chair that comes alive, the headless man, the man out of an empty room: science-fiction conventions listed. LO-4 rather than LO-1 for that reason.
'Griffin was rather a lawless person' is LO-13's own wording. Not LO-12: the item asks about his conduct, not about use versus misuse.
Assessing him as a scientist means weighing the discovery against what he did with it -- use against misuse. Not LO-13, which is the criminal record itself.
'Would you like to be invisible, and what are the advantages and disadvantages' is the power-and-responsibility question turned on the reader. Not LO-12: no discovery of Griffin's is being judged.
Invisible forces such as magnetism -- the science the fiction leans on. LO-4, since the item asks what the genre builds from; no outcome here covers physics, and that is worth saying.
Explicitly names science fiction and its prophetic imagination while asking whether invisibility is possible. The clearest LO-4 item in the chapter.
Names H.G. Wells. Extraction.
Completes the sentence with 'bare feet'. Extraction.
London. Extraction.
Dictionary meaning of 'bewildered'. No LO in this frame covers word-level vocabulary, so the competency is cited rather than stretching LO-1.
The boys were following a scientist. Extraction.
He was working on making bodies invisible. Extraction of the premise.
The gap filled is 'lawless', in the sentence that sets brilliance against it. LO-13's exact subject.
Burning the landlord's house is the lawless act itself. Not LO-1: the item's answer is the crime.
Transparent as glass. Extraction of the simile.
No clothes, no money, invisible. Extraction.
Mid-winter and no clothes. Extraction.
The big store. Extraction.
He escaped by shedding his clothes. Extraction; the trick is stated in the text.
A guest at the inn out of season. Extraction, though note the text makes the unusual season winter, not summer.
The reasons he gives for wanting no conversation -- solitude and work -- are his character as presented to Mrs Hall.
Meaning of 'eccentric'. Vocabulary, so the competency.
All three grounds for calling him eccentric together make the character impression. Not LO-1, since the key is 'all of the above'.
Mrs Hall tolerating him because he paid in advance characterises HER, which is why the chapter keeps asking it.
'What does the first encounter tell us about Mrs Hall' is character inference outright.
The strange incident is Griffin stealing while invisible -- the discovery turned to crime. Not LO-12: no comparison with proper use is asked.
The clergyman called it an extraordinary affair. Extraction.
'Spirits in the furniture' is the villagers reaching for the supernatural where the story supplies a scientific cause -- a convention of the genre. Not LO-1.
Meaning of 'hysterics'. Vocabulary, so the competency.
The robbery made the villagers suspect him. Extraction.
'Always quick-tempered' completes his character, not a plot fact.
Locates the theatrical shop. Extraction. DEFECT: the four options are spelling variants and the key selects 'Druy lane'; the text's street is Drury Lane, which is option B.
He stayed at an inn in Iping. Extraction.
Mrs Hall's verdict, 'eccentric'. Character through another character's eyes.
Shoes, overcoat, cold meat and sweets. Extraction.
Bitterly cold. Extraction; the same fact as the earlier winter item.
Two boys followed the footprints. Extraction.
Transparent as a sheet of glass. Extraction.
A medicine that made his body invisible. Extraction of the premise.
The paid-in-advance item again, in a second MCQ. Mrs Hall's character, treated as before.
He went on to Iping. Extraction.
Attacking and robbing the theatrical shopkeeper is one of the lawless acts LO-13 asks to be described.
He escaped by removing the new clothes. Extraction.
He was making an invisible man. Extraction of the premise.
'Griffin was a lawless man as he once...' -- burned the landlord's house. LO-13 stated as an MCQ.
Only mud betrays an invisible body: the rule the story invents and then obeys, which is how the genre works. Not LO-1.

Names the village he fled to. Extraction. DEFECT, and this is the known-bad one: the printed letter is A ('Lping') while the model answer reads '(c) Lping', and the real village is Iping -- option C's text. The option set carries an I/L typo from the source and no reading of it is correct as printed. Flagged, not fixed.
Mrs Hall was the landlord's wife. Extraction.
The second robbery, at the clergyman's. Another of the lawless acts, so LO-13 rather than bare recall.
The open guest-room door. Extraction.
Jaffers failing because the suspect turns invisible is the genre's set-piece -- the ordinary world defeated by the invented premise. Not LO-13.
'Brilliance fades before his darker traits' is exactly use against misuse of the discovery. Not LO-13 alone, because brilliance is half the question.
Griffin as the antithesis of the scientist who betters the world. The LO-12 comparison, framed as a proposition to justify.
Warmth, a bed, clothes. Extraction of his motive as stated.
Footprints with nobody making them -- the image the title takes and the genre's calling card. Not LO-1: the surprise is what is asked about.

MISFILED ITEM: this asks how Horace Danby read books after his arrest, which belongs to 'A Question of Trust' (chapter 23727), not to this story. Mapped on its own content as retrieval -- the prison librarian post -- because it must not be left unmapped, but it should be refiled by the publisher-side fix, not by a curriculum code.
Throwing off the bandages and striking everyone to escape an accusation is lawless conduct. Not LO-12.
Arson for revenge, and to bury the secret. The founding lawless act, and LO-13 asks what turns the scientist criminal.
How he got out of the store. Extraction.
Why the open door surprised them -- his room was always locked. Extraction.
Why no landlord would house him follows from the arson and the dislike he attracted. LO-13, the consequences of lawlessness.
The bandages, dark glasses, false nose, whiskers and hat. Extraction of the disguise.
The assault on the Halls and the unpaid rent are the grievances. Lawless conduct, not a character sketch.
Pairs the discovery with his nature in one item, which is the use-versus-misuse contrast plus characterisation.
The reasons he gave -- solitude, work, an accident to his face. Extraction, all stated.
Whether he responded to her friendliness is his character in company. Not LO-1: the item asks for a judgement.
Why he was suspected of the burglary -- the sudden cash after pleading poverty. The lawlessness catching up with him.
The disguise AND the assault on the shopkeeper. Lawless behaviour, not merely the costume.
How he shook off the store staff. Extraction.
Oversleeping, the chase, and back into the January cold without clothes. Extraction of the sequence.
Why Mrs Hall overlooked his habits. Her character, consistent with the MCQs on the same point.
What he did in the theatrical shop ends with striking and robbing the shopkeeper. LO-13.
'Trace the character arc' at five marks: the character across the story, and the descent into crime that the arc consists of.
A 120-word diary entry on misusing science and endangering society: LO-12's subject in the extended written form LO-3 measures. Not LO-14, which is the reader's verdict rather than Griffin's own.
A dialogue built from the cue about Mrs Hall's friendliness and his refusal -- both characters, written out. Not LO-13: no crime is involved.
'With great power comes great responsibility', justified in 120 words. LO-14's warning, named in the stem.
How he became visible and what drove him out again is retrieval across two episodes, at five marks. Not LO-12: no judgement is asked.
How the eccentric could be helped to live normally, and the values he lacks -- character plus the responsibility the story says he never accepted.
The headless man in the bar and the constable grappling with a vanishing suspect: the genre's spectacle, described at length. Not LO-13, since the scene is wonder rather than crime.
His appearance at the inn plus evidence of his irritable temper. A character question at five marks.
A letter as Jaffers about meeting an invisible man -- the genre's premise retold from inside the ordinary world.
'Arrest a man without a head' is the same convention as the bar scene, asked as narration.
The extract is the arrival at the inn; sub-item i asks for an inference about Griffin, the rest are retrieval from the passage. Character plus extraction, not LO-13.
The extract turns on a man appearing from an empty bedroom and a room thought haunted, and sub-item i asks why -- the genre's device, with retrieval alongside.
Every sub-item is retrieval from the printed extract: why 'fully dressed and visible', where he was, why he went there. The last is a vocabulary substitution, which no LO reaches.
The curious episode, why they crept downstairs, whom he told about the cheque -- retrieval from the extract throughout. Not LO-13: the theft is reported, not judged.
